doc.title: Randy Brecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 12, 2022

chapter: Michael, influences and the Brecker Brothers
title: Birth of the Brecker Brothers, Clive Davis and 'Sneaking Up Behind You'
summary: Clive Davis insisted on the Brecker Brothers name and a single; the band jammed up 'Sneaking Up Behind You', a 1975 R&B hit.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: friend Dave Sanborn who had just moved to New York or he was in Woodstock, he was close by. So that became an impetus for me to write — the cumulative effect of everything that had happened in my life, the music was the cumulative effect of everything that happened in my life both on the jazz side and on the jazz-rock or whatever you want to call it side. So I just got to work composing every day. And eventually we had rehearsals that a lot of the guys from the band Dreams — Will Lee on bass, Don Grolnick on keyboards, Steve Khan on guitar, Chris Parker on drums, me and Mike, Sanborn. We’d rehearse once or twice a week in one of their lofts. A lot of the cats lived in the same building and Grolnick was writing, Steve was writing, it wasn’t only my material but I had this thought in mind for this specific thing. Anyway to make a long story short, somehow the word about the band, the stuff we’d been writing, kind of filtered through the grapevine and I got a call from a guy named Steve Becker, who had just signed a production deal with Clive Davis, who had taken over a label called Bell Records and was changing it to Arista Records. Now Clive was a genius in the business. He had signed Dreams to Columbia Records and we did two semi-successful records for him. But this was — and then there was a kind of a scandal that went on and he was innocent but he got fired from Columbia Records so the fact that he was coming back now starting something new was an interesting situation. It was a caveat to his messenger, Steve Becker mentioned that he’ll sign you, you won’t have to do a demo, we were going to start doing demos, that’s what you had to do and try to talk companies into sending it. He said, “He’ll sign ya, we’ve heard about this music, but you have to call the band The Brecker Brothers.” And I, you know, duly protested, because I had worked on this music for a couple of years, it was supposed to be my solo record and there are three guys in the front line so if you call it The Brecker Brothers Sanborn’s going to look funny. I made up every excuse I could — it’ll look like the long lost cousin. But Clive stuck to his game and I agreed, okay, call it The Brecker Brothers. So that was really the birth of the Brecker Brothers and not only was that not quite enough for Clive, I had written nine tunes, among them “Skunk Funk” and tunes in that style. Clive had me to a meeting in his office and he said, “Young man,” this guy always knew what he wanted, “you need a single.” And I really hit the ceiling, man, ‘cause I said look, first of all you’re calling it The Brecker Brothers, it’s supposed to be my own music, we don’t have a single, we just recorded everything I wrote. Basically he said if you don’t do a single it ain’t comin’ out, baby. He was very diplomatic, as he was. And I loved the guy. We would really kind of butt heads, but he was great. So we go in the studio, I explained the situation to the cats, we go to our loft, we jammed up a tune in about four hours. Everybody contributed. It’s called “Sneaking Up Behind You.” Will thought of a little [sings a melody] sneaking up behind you. He thought of the little words. Mike and I © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

jammed up a little [scats] I can’t even do it anymore, but a little horn line. And the next thing we know, we go in, Clive was in the studio. He loved it. The tune shot to number 2 on the R&B charts. And that’s what really sold The Brecker Brothers so to speak because they became really popular and this was in 19 — what year was it — 1975. “Sneaking Up Behind You” and that’s what sold the record and started our whole career. And we spent the last — I have to say, this is not great to say, but in a way we spent the next five or six records trying to recreate another hit just to have one more because we saw what it did for us you know. Next thing I know we’re headlining or we’re opening the show for Chaka Khan or Parliament Funkadelic. It led to amazing things.
